beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — the hesitant writer types the framing a viewer arrives with, then corrects it. 'the truth' -> 'the token that followed' is the thesis. First cut used the multi-word trigger 'what is true', which the component never matches (it compares one whitespace token at a time), so the correction silently never happened.
beats.narration_text: Here is the claim in one breath. Training does not teach a model what is true. It teaches it what followed. I am going to show you that happening, with numbers you can rerun.

show.event: 'Training teaches a model' types on the cream page in serif
'the truth' completes the naive framing, as the voice says 'what is true'
'truth' is backspaced out
'token that followed' types in its place, landing on the spoken 'followed'

props.text:
Training teaches a model
the truth.

beats.role_note: FRAMEWORK beat — the objective stated as the chapter states it, before any example. Quotes are verbatim from Chapter 1 Part 1.
beats.narration_text: The chapter states the loop in four steps. Take a passage of text. Hide the next token. Ask the model for its distribution. Compare that distribution with the token that actually followed. Then nudge every parameter so the token that followed gets a little more probability. Nothing in that loop is told what is true.

show.event: step 1 lights — a passage of text appears with its last token hidden
step 2 lights — the hidden slot is marked
step 3 lights — a distribution bar fans out from the model
step 4 lights — the actual next token drops in and is compared
the nudge arrow fires back into the parameters, terracotta
a struck-through 'is it true?' check appears and greys out — no such step exists

props.spark: Four steps. None of them check.

beats.role_note: The constructed corpus. LABELLED CONSTRUCTED ON SCREEN — assignment requires constructed illustrations be labelled. Canberra is the true capital; Sydney is the frequent misconception.
beats.narration_text: So I built a corpus where the frequent answer is false. This is constructed — I invented it, it is not web text, and it says so on screen. One context: the capital of Australia is. Sydney follows seven times. Canberra, the true answer, follows three. Melbourne never follows.

show.event: the CONSTRUCTED banner lands first, before any data
the context line types: 'the capital of australia is ___'
sydney row builds to 7 tally marks
canberra row builds to 3 tally marks and takes the TRUE flag
melbourne row stays empty at 0
corpus frequencies resolve beneath — 0.70 / 0.30 / 0.00

props.spark: The frequent answer is the false one.

beats.role_note: WORKED EXAMPLE, step 0. Numbers verbatim from code/OUTPUT.txt: 0.3333 each, loss 1.0986 = ln 3.
beats.narration_text: Training starts with the weights at zero, so every token is equally likely. Point three three three each. The loss is one point zero nine eight six — that is the natural log of three, exactly what uniform over three options costs. Now run the loop.

show.event: three bars rise to equal height, each labelled 0.3333
the step counter reads 0
the loss readout lands on 1.0986
'= ln 3' annotates the loss in terracotta

beats.role_note: The mechanism MOVING — bars animate through the real reported steps 1, 5, 20, 100, 600 from code/OUTPUT.txt. This is the beat that shows rather than asserts.
beats.narration_text: Watch the bars. Step one, Sydney is already ahead. Step five, point five six. Step twenty, point six seven. By step six hundred it settles: Sydney point six nine nine, Canberra point two nine nine, Melbourne point zero zero two. The loss fell the whole way. Nothing checked a fact.

show.event: step counter ticks 1 — sydney bar pulls ahead
step 5 — sydney 0.5588, loss falls to 0.7858
step 20 — sydney 0.6726, melbourne collapsing
step 600 — bars settle at 0.6989 / 0.2989 / 0.0022
the loss trace beneath has fallen the whole way, unbroken

props.spark: The loss falls. Nothing is checked.

beats.role_note: The concept in two measured numbers, both from code/OUTPUT.txt: max gap from corpus 0.0022, max gap from truth 0.7011.
beats.narration_text: Here is the whole concept in two numbers. Distance from the corpus frequencies: zero point zero zero two two. Distance from the truth: zero point seven zero one one. The objective walked the model to within two thousandths of the corpus, and left it seven tenths away from the right answer. Argmax is Sydney.

show.event: the converged distribution sits at the top as the reference
left gauge measures distance to CORPUS — needle lands at 0.0022
right gauge measures distance to TRUTH — needle swings to 0.7011
the two numbers sit side by side, the truth gap in terracotta
'argmax = sydney · truth = canberra' resolves beneath

props.spark: 0.0022 from the corpus. 0.7011 from the truth.

beats.role_note: The loss floor — the objective is SATISFIED by a contradictory corpus. loss 0.6131 vs corpus entropy 0.6109, both from code/OUTPUT.txt.
beats.narration_text: One more thing the numbers show. The loss stops at zero point six one three one. It cannot reach zero, because the corpus contradicts itself about this context. The floor is the corpus's own entropy, zero point six one zero nine. A perfect fit to a wrong corpus is still a perfect fit.

show.event: the loss curve draws from 1.0986 downward
the curve flattens and stops short of zero at 0.6131
a dashed floor line draws in at 0.6109, labelled 'corpus entropy'
the gap between curve and zero is marked — it is not a bug
'a perfect fit to a wrong corpus is still a perfect fit' resolves

props.spark: It bottoms out at the corpus, not at zero.

beats.role_note: Closes the obvious objection — that RLHF fixes it. Quotes are verbatim from Chapter 1 Part 1. Uses the native TargetStack (word-cued, 1920x1080) instead of the library LayerStack, whose fixed reveal timing could not follow the voice and whose 1280x720 geometry left the frame under-filled. SCOPE NOTE: Chapter 1 lists preference tuning as its own concept. This beat does not teach it; it closes the obvious objection ('doesn't later training fix this?') using the chapter's own line that neither stage receives an answer key, then returns to the one concept.
beats.narration_text: You might think the later training stage fixes this. The chapter is blunt: neither stage receives an answer key. Preference tuning targets what raters approved of. Approval and correctness overlap, but where they diverge the signal follows approval. A confident, well organized, wrong answer is exactly what gets preferred.

show.event: card one stacks in — pretraining targets the observed token
card two stacks in — preference tuning targets rater approval
card three stacks in on a terracotta rail — neither receives an answer key
the caption settles beneath the stack

beats.role_note: REQUIRED BY THE ASSIGNMENT — names what the explanation does NOT establish. Three explicit limits, the middle one quoting the chapter's own statement about interpretability.
beats.narration_text: Here is what this does not establish. My corpus is three tokens and invented. This does not show that a real model's probabilities equal web frequencies — real models generalize, and the chapter says nobody can read off why a given prediction was made. It also does not show models are usually wrong. Only that truth was never the target.

show.event: the header 'what this does NOT establish' lands
limit one types in — a 3-token toy is not a language model
limit two types in — real probabilities are not web frequencies
limit three types in — this is not a claim that models are usually wrong
the single surviving claim resolves in terracotta beneath the three limits

beats.role_note: SCAFFOLDED TASK — the viewer flips the result by editing the corpus. Labelled reconstructed UI; the former reply lines were removed. The expected result is stated in the tag as what the script actually prints (verified: sydney=2 -> P(canberra)=0.5989, argmax canberra), not as a Claude answer.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. The script is in the folder. Change Sydney's count from seven to two and rerun it. Watch argmax flip to Canberra — not because the model learned a fact, but because you edited the corpus.
